study_identification_part.si4_title: Effects of anterior temporal lobe resection on cortical morphology

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study investigates the effects of anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR) on cortical morphology by comparing pre-surgical and post-surgical MRI scans using both traditional and independent morphological measures. The aim is to identify affected brain regions and understand the nature of these changes.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Surface-based statistical analysis using SurfStat (Matlab toolbox) with random field theory for multiple comparison correction; employed a design matrix to compare pre- and postoperative groups; tested for effects of covariates (age at surgery, duration since first seizure, resection volume, side of resection, time between surgery and postoperative scan, and seizure outcome) on subject-wise differences between pre- and postoperative data.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR) leads to widespread morphological changes, both ipsilaterally and contralaterally, in regions mainly near resections and those structurally connected to the anterior temporal lobe, with independent morphological measures revealing more pronounced effects than traditional measures.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Surgery significantly affected all morphological measures. Ipsilateral effects were observed in the orbitofrontal and inferior frontal gyri (changes in total surface area, exposed surface area, tension term K, isometric term I, and shape term S), lateral occipital gyrus and lingual cortex (changes in cortical thickness, exposed surface area, tension term K, and isometric term I), and pre- and postcentral gyri and supramarginal gyrus (thickness changes). Contralateral effects included the lateral occipital gyrus (thickness, total surface area, tension term K, and isometric term I) and the inferior frontal gyrus and frontal pole (total area, tension term K, and isometric term I). Independent morphological measures identified additional changes not found by traditional measures, such as in the supramarginal gyrus (K) and contralateral frontal pole (K, I). No significant effects of tested covariates (age at surgery, duration of TLE, resection volume, side of resection, time to postoperative scan, seizure outcome) were found on morphological changes.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Inability to decisively determine if morphological changes are due to atrophy, reorganisation, or compensatory plasticity; lack of data to test for differences in morphological changes based on language lateralization; inability to investigate cingulate cortex with independent morphometrics due to technical limitations.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: We cannot decisively determine if morphological change is a sign of atrophy or reorganisation, or potentially even increased function to compensate for the loss of tissue.; Due to lack of data, we did not test for differences in morphological changes when grouping subjects by language lateralisation...; Although we did not find significant changes to the cingulate cortex in the traditional morphometrics, we were unable to investigate this region with independent morphometrics due to limitations of t...

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study highlights the benefit of using independent morphological measures (K, I, S) to reveal subtle cortical changes that traditional measures might miss, particularly the tension term K due to its near-invariant value in controls.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study used a surface-based approach for increased sensitivity and excluded the entire ipsilateral temporal lobe from analysis to avoid resection morphology effects.
